tail.text: Walk me through how the export job picks the lines for a day. I want to be sure nothing is counted twice.

The fetch step asks the ledger for every posting whose booking time falls in the export day, in UTC, for one legal entity at a time. It orders them by posting id and reads them in pages of 5,000, remembering the last id of each page and asking for the ids after it, so a posting that arrives while the job runs either falls into a page or comes after the last one; it is never read twice. Reversals are separate postings with their own id and a negative amount, so they show up as lines of their own rather than changing an earlier line. The write step then turns the postings into CSV lines in the same order. Nothing in this path deduplicates, because nothing in it can duplicate. I only read the code.
Why does the month-end export take 40 minutes when a normal day takes three?
fetch 36 m 40 s; write 2 m 10 s; upload 0 m 50 s

The time goes into the fetch step: 36 minutes of the 40. At month end the ledger holds about twelve times the usual number of postings for the last day, because the accruals and the closing entries are booked then, and the query that reads them uses the index on booking time but then sorts by posting id in memory. With a combined index on entity, booking time and posting id the sort would disappear. I tried the query plan on a copy of the database: with that index the month-end fetch would take about 4 minutes. The index is a change to the ledger schema, which belongs to the ledger team, so I did not create it.
What happens when the upload to the bucket fails halfway?

The upload writes the file under a temporary name first. Only when every byte is written and the checksum the bucket reports matches the one we computed does the job rename it to its final name. A failure in the middle leaves a temporary file behind, which the bucket removes by itself after a day, and the job retries up to five times with growing waits, from 10 seconds to about 3 minutes. If all five tries fail, the job exits with an error and the alert goes to the finance on-call channel. Finance never sees a half-written file under a final name, because the rename is the last step. I changed nothing.
For converting amounts in a foreign currency to the entity currency: should halves round up, or round to even?
Round to even. That is what the finance tool does, and the totals must match theirs to the cent.
ok  finance/export/jobs/export 2.3s

Converted amounts now round half to even, and a new test checks the totals of a sample month against the figures from the finance tool: they match to the cent. The verify command exists as a draft on my branch; it reads the signature file but cannot check it until the public key is published.
Which columns does finance actually use? I suspect half of them are never read.

From the import mapping finance shared last month, they read 11 of the 17 columns: posting id, booking date, account number, entity, currency, amount in minor units, amount in entity currency, counter account, document number, cost centre and the reversal flag. The other six, among them the created-by field and the two internal batch ids, map to nothing on their side. Dropping them would make each file about a third smaller, but the format rule says every change is announced a week ahead, and a removed column could break some script elsewhere that we do not know of. I would ask before removing anything; no change made.
How does the golden file test decide that an export is right?

The test runs the whole export for a fixed day against a small seeded ledger of 240 postings, then compares the produced file with the stored golden file line by line. Any difference fails the test and prints the first ten lines that differ. The seeded ledger covers the awkward cases on purpose: a posting exactly at midnight, a reversal, an amount of zero, a posting in a foreign currency and an account number with leading zeros. When the format changes on purpose, the golden file is regenerated with a flag and the difference is reviewed in the merge request like any other change. I only read the test.
Explain the plan for signing in plain words, so I can tell finance.

Each export file gets a second, small file next to it with the same name and the ending .sig. That file holds a signature made with the private key of the legal entity. Anyone with the matching public key can check that the export came from our job and was not changed afterwards, not even by one character. The private keys live only in the signing service, and the export job asks that service to sign a checksum of the file; it never sees a key. Finance needs the public keys once, and their tool can then check every file on import and refuse one that does not match. That is the plan as the ceremony notes describe it.

tail.text: Explain how a probe decides when to wake the radio. I want to understand it before anyone touches the scheduler again.

A probe keeps its radio off almost all the time. Each reading goes into a ring buffer in RAM. When the buffer holds 12 readings, or when a reading crosses one of the alarm limits for temperature or moisture, the scheduler raises the radio flag. On the next timer tick the radio is powered, the probe listens for 30 milliseconds to make sure the channel is free, sends the batch, and waits up to 200 milliseconds for the gateway to acknowledge it. Without an acknowledgement the batch stays in the buffer and leaves with the next one, so nothing is lost unless the buffer overflows, which takes about two days of silence. After the send the radio is powered down again. I changed nothing; this describes the code on the main branch.
A probe at the north silo rebooted four times last night. Find out why if you can, but do not change anything yet.
4 resets, cause: brown-out, battery 2.61 V at -9 C

The resets are brown-outs, not crashes. That probe has an older cell, and at minus nine degrees its voltage sags to 2.61 volts under load, which is below the 2.7 volt brown-out level of the board. Each time the radio powers up, the extra current pulls the cell under the limit and the board resets. After the reset the probe comes back, the buffered readings are still in flash, and the next send succeeds once the cell has recovered a little. So the probe loses a few minutes of readings but nothing that was already stored. The real cure is a fresh cell; a firmware change could lower the radio power on cold nights, but that trades away range, and we should decide it together. Nothing is changed.
How long will the flash last if every probe keeps 48 hours of readings?

The flash chip on revision C is rated for 100,000 erase cycles per sector. At the current sampling rate a probe writes about 60 readings a day on average, each of 16 bytes. The 48 hour ring spans 6 sectors, and each sector is erased once every time the ring wraps around, roughly every two days. That makes about 180 erases per sector per year, which is far from the rating: the flash outlives the battery holder, the board and probably the silo. The only thing that would wear it out fast is a bug that rewrites one sector in a loop, which is why the write path keeps a counter that goes out in the health packet. No change made.
Can you do the battery voltage in the health packet today? Revision C first.
58 tests passed

Done for revision C. Because the ADC on the revision C board shares its reference with the radio, I had to take the battery reading in the quiet window right after the radio goes to sleep, and with that change the probes now report battery voltage in the health packet, accurate to within 20 millivolts against the bench supply, and all 58 tests pass on the board. Revision B has a different ADC pin and still sends no voltage.
How does the bootloader decide which image to start after an update?

There are two image slots. The bootloader reads a small header at the start of each slot: a version, a length, a signature and a flag that says whether that image has ever booted successfully. It starts the newest image whose signature checks out. A freshly written image starts on trial: if the application does not confirm itself within 60 seconds of booting, by setting the success flag after its first good radio exchange, the watchdog resets the board and the bootloader falls back to the other slot. That is how a broken image rolls back on its own. The signature check uses the public key compiled into the bootloader, which cannot be changed in the field. This is a description; nothing was edited.
Why does the firmware build take so long on the build machine? It used to be quick.
total 6 m 12 s; link-time optimisation 4 m 50 s

Almost all of the time is link-time optimisation: 4 minutes 50 of the 6 minutes 12. It was switched on for the release profile, which is right because it saves about 9 percent of flash, but the nightly build and the developer builds use the release profile as well. A debug profile without it would build in under a minute and a half. Release images would keep the optimisation, so nothing changes for what goes onto the probes. I have not touched the build files; tell me if you want the separate profile.
What is the packet loss at the east silo this week compared to last week?

Packet loss at the east silo went from 3.1 percent last week to 7.4 percent this week. All of the increase comes from the six probes on the far side of the new grain bin that went up on Tuesday: the metal bin now stands between them and the gateway. The probes resend whatever was not acknowledged, so no reading is lost yet, but they wake the radio more often and their battery forecast fell by about a month. Raising the gateway two metres or adding a repeater would fix it; both are hardware questions for the site. I only read the statistics.

Explain how the alias switch works during a reindex.

The reindex job writes into a fresh index whose name carries the date and time. Queries keep going to the alias, which points at the old index the whole time. When the new index holds every document and its count matches the database within a tenth of a percent, the job runs a set of sample queries against both indexes and compares the top results. Only if they agree well enough does it move the alias in one atomic step, so a query sees either the old index or the new one, never a mix. The old index stays for a day in case the alias has to move back. Nothing was changed; this is how the job is written.

tail.text: How does a freed slot reach a waiting patient today, step by step?

When a booking is cancelled, the booking service emits a slot release event with the clinic, the time and the kind of appointment. The offer then goes to the sender, which writes the message. If the patient accepts, the slot becomes their booking; if they decline, the next patient in line gets the offer. tail.text: Why does the month-end export take 40 minutes when a normal day takes three?
fetch 36 m 40 s; write 2 m 10 s; upload 0 m 50 s

The time goes into the fetch step: 36 minutes of the 40. At month end the ledger holds about twelve times the usual number of postings for the last day, because the accruals and the closing entries are booked then, and the query that reads them uses the index on booking time but then sorts by posting id in memory. With a combined index on entity, booking time and posting id the sort would disappear. I tried the query plan on a copy of the database: with that index the month-end fetch would take about 4 minutes. The index is a change to the ledger schema, which belongs to the ledger team, so I did not create it.
Which columns does finance actually use? I suspect half of them are never read.

From the import mapping finance shared last month, they read 11 of the 17 columns: posting id, booking date, account number, entity, currency, amount in minor units, amount in entity currency, counter account, document number, cost centre and the reversal flag. The other six, among them the created-by field and the two internal batch ids, map to nothing on their side. Dropping them would make each file about a third smaller, but the format rule says every change is announced a week ahead, and a removed column could break some script elsewhere that we do not know of. I would ask before removing anything; no change made.
Walk me through how the export job picks the lines for a day. I want to be sure nothing is counted twice.

The fetch step asks the ledger for every posting whose booking time falls in the export day, in UTC, for one legal entity at a time. It orders them by posting id and reads them in pages of 5,000, remembering the last id of each page and asking for the ids after it, so a posting that arrives while the job runs either falls into a page or comes after the last one; it is never read twice. Reversals are separate postings with their own id and a negative amount, so they show up as lines of their own rather than changing an earlier line. The write step then turns the postings into CSV lines in the same order. Nothing in this path deduplicates, because nothing in it can duplicate. I only read the code.
Status on the bucket move?
wrote 2026-11-11-entity1.csv and 2026-11-11-entity1.csv.sig to the new bucket

The exports now go to the new bucket instead of the old one: last night the run wrote the file and its signature there, and the old bucket received nothing. The first legal entity is signed; the second still writes unsigned files because its key is not created yet. One more thing you should know: the service account that writes to the new bucket has a key that expires on 1 December, and the job fails without it.
What happens when the upload to the bucket fails halfway?

The upload writes the file under a temporary name first. Only when every byte is written and the checksum the bucket reports matches the one we computed does the job rename it to its final name. A failure in the middle leaves a temporary file behind, which the bucket removes by itself after a day, and the job retries up to five times with growing waits, from 10 seconds to about 3 minutes. If all five tries fail, the job exits with an error and the alert goes to the finance on-call channel. Finance never sees a half-written file under a final name, because the rename is the last step. I changed nothing.
How does the golden file test decide that an export is right?

The test runs the whole export for a fixed day against a small seeded ledger of 240 postings, then compares the produced file with the stored golden file line by line. Any difference fails the test and prints the first ten lines that differ. The seeded ledger covers the awkward cases on purpose: a posting exactly at midnight, a reversal, an amount of zero, a posting in a foreign currency and an account number with leading zeros. When the format changes on purpose, the golden file is regenerated with a flag and the difference is reviewed in the merge request like any other change. I only read the test.
Explain the plan for signing in plain words, so I can tell finance.

Each export file gets a second, small file next to it with the same name and the ending .sig. That file holds a signature made with the private key of the legal entity. Anyone with the matching public key can check that the export came from our job and was not changed afterwards, not even by one character. The private keys live only in the signing service, and the export job asks that service to sign a checksum of the file; it never sees a key. Finance needs the public keys once, and their tool can then check every file on import and refuse one that does not match. That is the plan as the ceremony notes describe it.

tail.text: Explain how the alias switch works during a reindex.

The reindex job writes into a fresh index whose name carries the date and time. Queries keep going to the alias, which points at the old index the whole time. When the new index holds every document and its count matches the database within a tenth of a percent, the job runs a set of sample queries against both indexes and compares the top results. Only if they agree well enough does it move the alias in one atomic step, so a query sees either the old index or the new one, never a mix. The old index stays for a day in case the alias has to move back. Nothing was changed; this is how the job is written.

Neither catalogue has been reindexed with the new analyzer yet; both reindex jobs wait for the next quiet night.

How does a freed slot reach a waiting patient today, step by step?

When a booking is cancelled, the booking service emits a slot release event with the clinic, the time and the kind of appointment. The waiting list service picks the patient who has waited longest for that kind of appointment at that clinic and marks the slot as offered to them, so nobody else can be offered it at the same moment. tail.text: How does the bootloader decide which image to start after an update?

There are two image slots. The bootloader reads a small header at the start of each slot: a version, a length, a signature and a flag that says whether that image has ever booted successfully. It starts the newest image whose signature checks out. A freshly written image starts on trial: if the application does not confirm itself within 60 seconds of booting, by setting the success flag after its first good radio exchange, the watchdog resets the board and the bootloader falls back to the other slot. That is how a broken image rolls back on its own. The signature check uses the public key compiled into the bootloader, which cannot be changed in the field. This is a description; nothing was edited.
A probe at the north silo rebooted four times last night. Find out why if you can, but do not change anything yet.
4 resets, cause: brown-out, battery 2.61 V at -9 C

The resets are brown-outs, not crashes. That probe has an older cell, and at minus nine degrees its voltage sags to 2.61 volts under load, which is below the 2.7 volt brown-out level of the board. Each time the radio powers up, the extra current pulls the cell under the limit and the board resets. After the reset the probe comes back, the buffered readings are still in flash, and the next send succeeds once the cell has recovered a little. So the probe loses a few minutes of readings but nothing that was already stored. The real cure is a fresh cell; a firmware change could lower the radio power on cold nights, but that trades away range, and we should decide it together. Nothing is changed.
What is the packet loss at the east silo this week compared to last week?

Packet loss at the east silo went from 3.1 percent last week to 7.4 percent this week. All of the increase comes from the six probes on the far side of the new grain bin that went up on Tuesday: the metal bin now stands between them and the gateway. The probes resend whatever was not acknowledged, so no reading is lost yet, but they wake the radio more often and their battery forecast fell by about a month. Raising the gateway two metres or adding a repeater would fix it; both are hardware questions for the site. I only read the statistics.
Last question before the release build: which signing key does 2.4 use, the 2025 key or the new one from the ceremony?
The new key from the ceremony. The 2025 key gets revoked after this release.

Understood, 2.4 is signed with the new key from the ceremony. I checked both gateways while waiting for the build: they still run the 2.3 radio stack, and the update package for them is not built yet.
Explain how a probe decides when to wake the radio. I want to understand it before anyone touches the scheduler again.

A probe keeps its radio off almost all the time. Each reading goes into a ring buffer in RAM. When the buffer holds 12 readings, or when a reading crosses one of the alarm limits for temperature or moisture, the scheduler raises the radio flag. On the next timer tick the radio is powered, the probe listens for 30 milliseconds to make sure the channel is free, sends the batch, and waits up to 200 milliseconds for the gateway to acknowledge it. Without an acknowledgement the batch stays in the buffer and leaves with the next one, so nothing is lost unless the buffer overflows, which takes about two days of silence. After the send the radio is powered down again. I changed nothing; this describes the code on the main branch.
How long will the flash last if every probe keeps 48 hours of readings?

The flash chip on revision C is rated for 100,000 erase cycles per sector. At the current sampling rate a probe writes about 60 readings a day on average, each of 16 bytes. The 48 hour ring spans 6 sectors, and each sector is erased once every time the ring wraps around, roughly every two days. That makes about 180 erases per sector per year, which is far from the rating: the flash outlives the battery holder, the board and probably the silo. The only thing that would wear it out fast is a bug that rewrites one sector in a loop, which is why the write path keeps a counter that goes out in the health packet. No change made.
Why does the firmware build take so long on the build machine? It used to be quick.
total 6 m 12 s; link-time optimisation 4 m 50 s

Almost all of the time is link-time optimisation: 4 minutes 50 of the 6 minutes 12. It was switched on for the release profile, which is right because it saves about 9 percent of flash, but the nightly build and the developer builds use the release profile as well. A debug profile without it would build in under a minute and a half. Release images would keep the optimisation, so nothing changes for what goes onto the probes. I have not touched the build files; tell me if you want the separate profile.
